t: Come to the Throne of Grace at Any Time
v: Having then a great high priest, who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold tightly to our confession.
For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.
Let us therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy, and may find grace for help in time of need.
b: Jesus is not only the exalted Lord on high; he is also a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses. He truly became a man and experienced weariness, hunger, rejection, pain, and temptation, yet did not sin. So when we are weak, we need not be afraid to come before him. He knows exactly what we are going through. True faith is not pretending we have no weakness, but coming to Jesus even in our weakness.
The focus is not on “how weak I am,” but on “who Jesus is.”

We often think we must perform better or become more spiritual before we are qualified to draw near to God, but the gospel is exactly the opposite. Hebrews says, “Let us therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace.” We can draw near to God not because we are good enough, but because Jesus has opened the way for us. When we admit our limits and let go of the self-centeredness of trying to solve everything by ourselves, we can return to our rightful place as human beings, letting God be God and Jesus be King. It is not that we overcome weakness by ourselves, but that in grace Christ becomes our strength.

The throne of grace is not a place that condemns us, but a place to “receive mercy, and find grace for help.” What is especially precious is “in time of need”: not only in success but also in failure; not only when we are strong but also when we are weakest. When temptation comes, when the heart is weary, when circumstances are hard, our first reaction should not be to grit our teeth and carry on by ourselves, but to turn to Jesus at once. Draw near to the Lord at any time, draw on grace at any time, and overcome by the Lord at any time.
a: Come to Jesus in Weakness
Don’t run from God, and don’t tough it out alone.
Receive Grace Boldly
We draw near to God not by our performance but through Jesus.
Ask the Lord for Help at Any Time
Bring every need, temptation, and difficulty to God right away.
q: When I am weak, fail, or face difficulty, is my first reaction to rely on myself or to come to Jesus for grace?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving Jesus to be my high priest, who fully knows and sympathizes with my weakness. Help me no longer to tough it out on my own, but to come to the throne of grace at any time. I will let Jesus be King, and by the Holy Spirit receive Your mercy, grace, and help, and overcome by the Lord in every circumstance. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, to receive mercy, find grace, and have help at any time!

t: In a Dry Land, Thirsting More Deeply for God
v: (A Psalm by David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah.) God, you are my God. I will earnestly seek you. My soul thirsts for you. My flesh longs for you, in a dry and weary land, where there is no water.
So I have seen you in the sanctuary, to see your power and your glory.
Because your loving kindness is better than life, my lips shall praise you.
So I will bless you while I live. I will lift up my hands in your name.
My soul shall be satisfied as with the richest food. My mouth shall praise you with joyful lips,
[Combined with the previous verse.]
for you have been my help. I will rejoice in the shadow of your wings.
My soul stays close to you. Your right hand holds me up.
b: When David wrote this psalm he was in the wilderness of Judah, in “a dry and weary land,” yet his deepest desire was not to leave the wilderness first, but “My soul thirsts for you. My flesh longs for you.” This is a very deep lesson in the spiritual life: the drier the circumstances, the more we must seek God; the wearier the life, the more we must draw near to God.

Often we ask God to change our circumstances first, but David first sought God himself. The focus is not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances, but on Jesus; for what can truly satisfy us is not only the blessings God gives, but God himself.

David said, “Your loving kindness is better than life.” What he wanted was not merely for God to solve his problems, but for God’s presence. Even in the night watches when he could not sleep, he still remembered God and meditated on him, and as a result his soul moved from thirst to satisfaction. The outer wilderness did not vanish at once, but the inner life changed first. This reminds us that change does not always begin with circumstances; it begins with the heart.
When we lay down our anxiety and need to control, let God be God and Jesus be King, the Holy Spirit can bring a dry heart to fresh fullness.

Finally David said, “My soul stays close to you. Your right hand holds me up.” This is a beautiful picture: on one side, we cling to God; on the other, God’s strong right hand holds us up. Faith is not merely our own effort to hold on to God; it is God who keeps holding us up. I follow him, and he upholds me; I look to him, and he becomes my strength.
Even if our circumstances are still a wilderness, as long as God is with us, the wilderness can become a place to know and experience God more deeply.
a: Seek God All the More in Dry Times
Don’t flee the circumstances first; return to God’s presence first.
Long for God More Than His Blessings
Ask not only what God can do for me, but desire God himself.
Cling to God
Let Jesus be King each day, and trust that God’s right hand will hold you up.
q: In my present “wilderness,” what do I long for most: a change of circumstances, or to gain God himself more deeply?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, You are my God, and I will earnestly seek You. Even in a dry and weary land, let my heart still long for You and look to You. I will lay down self, let Jesus be King in me, and by the Holy Spirit cling closely to You. Thank You that Your loving kindness is better than life and that Your right hand will hold me up, so that my heart may be truly satisfied in You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will earnestly seek my God; my soul clings to him, and his right hand will hold me up!

t: Gaining Christ Surpasses Everything
v: “The Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found, and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field.
Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a merchant seeking fine pearls,
who, having found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had, and bought it.”
b: Jesus uses “treasure hidden in the field” and “one pearl of great price” to show the incomparable value of the Kingdom of Heaven. After finding the treasure, the man sells all that he has “in his joy,” because he knows what he gains is far more precious than what he gives up. This is not a painful loss but a joyful exchange. When we truly see the glory of God’s Kingdom, we will understand that letting go for the Lord is not losing but gaining a far greater treasure.
The key is not how much we give up, but how precious we see Jesus and his Kingdom to be.

The reason people hold on to themselves and will not let go is often that they have not yet truly seen the fullness of Christ. A self-centered life wants to grip what is “mine”: my rights, my interests, my reputation, my plans. But the gospel lets us see that true abundance is not “how much I own” but “whether I have gained Christ.” When we are willing to lay down self and let Jesus be King, we discover that selflessness is not having nothing, but letting go of our limited self and entering the limitless fullness of Christ.

Both parables share the same action: “sells all that he has.” Jesus is not teaching that salvation can be bought with possessions; salvation is God’s free grace. What is emphasized here is that the Kingdom is worth our total commitment. Whoever truly meets Christ will find the order of life’s values changed: no longer letting self be king, but letting Jesus be King; no longer treating the temporary things of earth as everything, but seeing today from eternity. God gives me, and I give for God; I lay down myself, and I gain Christ; gaining Christ, I gain true abundance.
a: See the Value of the Kingdom Anew
Don’t let temporary things hide the eternal treasure.
Gladly Lay Down Self
Lay down your rights, your face, and your sovereignty, and let Jesus be King.
Make Christ Your Greatest Treasure
Want not only the Lord’s blessings but the Lord himself.
q: What in my life am I clinging to that keeps me from following Jesus more fully?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, open my eyes to see how precious Your Kingdom and Jesus Christ are. Help me no longer to cling to myself and the temporary things of earth, but to gladly lay down self and let Jesus be King. Let me make Christ my greatest treasure, follow You all my life, and live out Your will, so that all glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I gladly let go of everything, to gain the treasure of the Kingdom!

t: When Afraid, Look to God Again
v: David arose and fled that day for fear of Saul, and went to Achish the king of Gath.
The servants of Achish said to him, “Isn’t this David the king of the land? Didn’t they sing one to another about him in dances, saying, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands’?”
David laid up these words in his heart, and was very afraid of Achish the king of Gath.
He changed his behavior before them, and pretended to be insane in their hands, and scribbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down on his beard.
Then Achish said to his servants, “Look, you see the man is mad. Why then have you brought him to me?
Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to play the madman in my presence? Shall this fellow come into my house?”
b: David once bravely faced Goliath, but now, fleeing from Saul, he came to the Philistine city of Gath, Goliath’s hometown. When Achish’s servants recognized him, David “laid up these words in his heart, and was very afraid,” and even pretended to be insane to survive. This shows us that even great men of faith have moments of weakness. Winning by faith yesterday does not mean we will not be afraid today, so we need to rely on God afresh every day.
True victory is not never having fear, but turning to God again in the midst of fear.

The passage specifically says David “laid up these words in his heart,” and so he was greatly afraid. What occupies the heart easily shapes the life. When our focus is only on Saul, Achish, and the dangerous circumstances, fear grows larger; when our focus returns to God, faith can stand up again. According to the heading of Psalm 34, David later looked back on this experience and declared, “I sought Yahweh, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears.” The focus is not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances; the focus must return to God.

God did not give up on David because of a moment of weakness. This humiliating experience actually helped David know more deeply that true safety is not in his own cleverness or in the protection of others, but in God. Human methods can only solve problems temporarily, but God shapes our lives through circumstances. When we see our own limits, we no longer need to be our own king, but can humbly return to God, letting Jesus be King and the Holy Spirit guide. Weakness is not the end; as long as we turn to God again, fear can become the starting point of deeper trust in him.
a: Turn to God When Afraid
Don’t let fear control you; return to God at once.
Guard Your Heart
Don’t magnify people’s words and circumstances; keep God’s word in your heart.
Rely on God Again in Weakness
Don’t seek safety through your own methods; let God be your true security.
q: What people, matters, or circumstances are making me afraid now? How can I turn my focus back to God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when I am afraid, help me not to be controlled by people’s words and circumstances, but to look to You again. I admit my limits and lay down my own methods, and let Jesus be King in me. Lead me, Holy Spirit, so that even in fear I choose to trust You and experience You as my salvation and my security. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I sought Yahweh, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears!

t: Living on Earth, with the Heart in Heaven
v: Brothers, be imitators together of me, and note those who walk this way, even as you have us for a pattern.
For many walk, of whom I told you often, and now tell you even weeping, as the enemies of the cross of Christ,
whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who think about earthly things.
For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ;
who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.
b: Paul sets two kinds of lives before us: one that “thinks about earthly things,” and another that knows “our citizenship is in heaven.” The problem is not that Christians may not handle work, family, and responsibilities on earth, but what is really the center of our lives.

When people live only for their own desires, interests, and pleasures, “the belly” becomes their god; but those who belong to Christ, though living on earth, have their lives governed by the King of heaven. When we change our viewpoint, we change our mindset; when we turn from an earthly viewpoint to a heavenly one, the order of life’s values is rearranged.

“Our citizenship is in heaven” is not only a hope of going to heaven someday; it means that today we already belong to another Kingdom. Since Jesus is King, we no longer make ourselves the center, but let him reign in our lives. The world asks, “What’s in it for me?” The life of the Kingdom asks, “Lord, what pleases you?” Selflessness is not leaving reality; it is, within real life, no longer letting self be king, and letting Jesus be King.
We still work, live, and build relationships, but we live on earth by the values of the Kingdom of Heaven.

We are still “waiting for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” to come from heaven. So the Christian life is not aimless walking toward death, but meeting Christ with a hope of glory. Our present bodies will decay, and everything on earth will pass away, but the Lord will make us like his glorious body. When we look at today from eternity, many things we could not let go of become small, and what truly matters becomes clear. Live on earth with your heart in heaven; be faithful today, and prepare to meet Jesus.
a: See Today with Heaven’s Eyes
Think not only about immediate gain and loss, but about eternal value.
Let Jesus Be King
Don’t let desires and self rule; choose each day the road that pleases God.
Live with Hope
Be faithful in today, and prepare for the return of the Lord Jesus.
q: Lately, are the things I care about and pursue most the temporary things of earth, or things of eternal Kingdom value?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for making me a citizen of heaven in Christ. Change my vision, so that I do not think only about earthly things but live from a heavenly, eternal point of view. Help me lay down self and let Jesus be King, by the Holy Spirit faithfully live out the life of the Kingdom, and wait with hope for the return of the Lord Jesus, so that my whole life may glorify You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am a citizen of heaven, and I wait for my Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, to come from heaven!

t: Let the Holy Spirit Lead My Life
v: But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’
But because I have told you these things, sorrow has filled your heart.
Nevertheless I tell you the truth: It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I don’t go away, the Counselor won’t come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you.
When he has come, he will convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment;
about sin, because they don’t believe in me;
about righteousness, because I am going to my Father, and you won’t see me anymore;
about judgment, because the prince of this world has been judged.
“I have yet many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now.

However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you the things that are coming.
He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you.
All things whatever the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he takes from what is mine, and will declare it to you.”
b: When the disciples heard that Jesus was about to leave, “sorrow filled their hearts,” because they saw only what they were losing right then; but Jesus said, “It is to your advantage that I go away.” People’s eyes often stay on the present, while God sees the whole plan. Jesus’ departure was not the end of God’s presence but the beginning of the Holy Spirit coming to dwell in believers. When we cannot make sense of our circumstances, let’s not rush to draw conclusions by our own judgment; let’s believe that God sees farther than we do.
The focus is not on how circumstances change, but on the fact that God is still in control.

Jesus calls the Holy Spirit “the Spirit of truth,” who comes to “guide you into all the truth.” The Spirit’s guidance does not replace the Bible, nor does it rely on feelings alone; it enables us to understand, receive, and live out God’s truth. The human mind can know many doctrines, but real change of life requires the Holy Spirit to bring truth into us, so that information becomes revelation, revelation brings conviction, and conviction produces practice. The Bible is my standard, and the Holy Spirit is my guide; not deciding for myself, but letting the Holy Spirit lead me into God’s heart.

Jesus states the highest purpose of the Spirit’s work very clearly: “He will glorify me.” Work that truly comes from the Holy Spirit does not put the spotlight on people; it makes people see Jesus more, obey Jesus more, and live out Jesus more. The Holy Spirit does not come to help “me be king,” but to make Jesus King in me. When we lay down our own wishes, abilities, and glory, and let the Holy Spirit lead, we can live out the life of Christ. The Holy Spirit leads me, Jesus is King in me, and in the end all glory goes to Jesus.
a: Trust God Even When You Can’t See
Don’t let present circumstances decide your faith.
Seek the Spirit’s Leading Daily
Take the Bible as your standard, and in prayer discern and obey God’s heart.
Let Jesus Receive the Glory in All Things
To tell whether something is from the Holy Spirit, ask: does it lift up Jesus?
q: In my life and decisions today, am I deciding for myself, or truly letting the Spirit of truth lead me?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for sending the Spirit of truth to dwell in me. Help me not to rely on my own cleverness and judgment, but to take Your Word as my standard and be sensitive to the leading of the Holy Spirit. Help me lay down my own sovereignty and let Jesus be King in me, so that my thoughts, choices, life, and service all follow Your heart, and all glory goes to Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The Spirit of truth will guide me into all the truth, so that my life glorifies Jesus!

t: Let God’s Word Bear Fruit in Your Heart
v: When a great multitude came together, and people from every city were coming to him, he spoke by a parable.
“The farmer went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the road, and it was trampled under foot, and the birds of the sky devoured it.
Other seed fell on the rock, and as soon as it grew, it withered away, because it had no moisture.
Other fell amongst the thorns, and the thorns grew with it and choked it.
Other fell into the good ground, and grew, and brought forth fruit one hundred times.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!”
His disciples asked him, “What does this parable mean?”
He said, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables, that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.
Those along the road are those who hear, then the devil comes, and takes away the word from their heart, that they may not believe and be saved.
Those on the rock are those who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but these have no root, who believe for a while, then fall away in time of temptation.
That which fell amongst the thorns, these are those who have heard, and as they go on their way they are choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and bring no fruit to maturity.
That in the good ground, these are such as in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and bring forth fruit with patience.”
b: Jesus explains it plainly: “The seed is the word of God.” The same seed sown on different soils yields completely different results; the difference lies not in the seed but in the soil. In the same way, God’s Word itself has life and power, and the key is the kind of heart with which we receive it. A heart like the roadside lets the truth be snatched away quickly; a heart like the rock may be moved for a moment but has no root; a heart like the thorns is filled with cares, riches, and pleasures. What really needs to change is not God’s Word but our hearts.

Jesus specifically points out that the thorns “choke” the word of God. Often it is not that we don’t want God, but that our hearts are already stuffed with too many things: worries, work, money, desires, people’s opinions, and our own plans. When “self” fills the heart, God’s Word has no room to reign. So growth in life is not only “knowing more” but letting the Holy Spirit shine his light on us, remove the stones and thorns in our hearts, and lay down our own sovereignty. The Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide, and Jesus is my example; let Jesus be King in the heart, and truth can move from knowledge into life.

Good soil does not merely “hear the word” but, “having heard the word, hold it tightly, and bring forth fruit with patience.” This is a process of growing life: hearing truth, receiving truth, believing truth, practicing truth, and then, through repeated practice, finally bearing fruit in life. God’s purpose is not to make us people who only listen to sermons, but to let his Word become life in us, and from life flow into daily living, relationships, and service. The sign of good soil is not how many sermons we have heard but how much fruit our lives bear; and the true fruit is increasingly living out Christ.
a: Tend the Soil of Your Heart Daily
Ask the Holy Spirit to shine light and remove hardness, shallowness, and thorns.
Practice the Truth You Hear
Don’t stop at knowing; live out God’s Word in daily life.
Persevere Until Life Bears Fruit
Don’t chase a moment’s feeling; keep rooting in Christ and let life gradually mature.
q: Today is my heart more like the roadside, the rock, the thorns, or the good soil? What is “choking” God’s Word and keeping my life from bearing fruit?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, make my heart good soil. Shine Your light on me, Holy Spirit, and remove the hardness, stones, and thorns in my heart, so that I not only hear Your Word but believe it, hold it fast, and truly obey it. I will lay down self and let Jesus be King in me, so that Your Word takes deep root in my life and bears abundant fruit, living out the life of Christ, and all glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will hold God’s Word fast in an honest and good heart, and bring forth fruit with patience!

t: Trusting God, the Heart Is at Peace
v: You will keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is steadfast, because he trusts in you.
Trust in Yahweh forever; for in Yah, Yahweh, is an everlasting Rock.
For he has brought down those who dwell on high, the lofty city. He lays it low. He lays it low even to the ground. He brings it even to the dust.
The foot shall tread it down: even the feet of the poor, and the steps of the needy.”
The way of the just is uprightness. You who are upright make the path of the righteous level.
b: The secret of “perfect peace” is not that circumstances have no problems, but that we are “steadfast” in trusting God. The Hebrew word for “peace” is shalom, and verse 3 doubles it, “peace, peace,” to express a complete and deep peace. The world outside may be shaken, yet the heart inside can be at rest, because true peace is not built on “everything going as I want” but on “God is still in control.” If our focus is on circumstances, the heart rises and falls with them; if our focus is on God, the heart is steadied by God.

Why can we trust God forever? Because “Yahweh is an everlasting Rock.” People change, circumstances change, and our own abilities change, but God never changes. We often become anxious because we want to control the unknown; but faith is laying down self as king and entrusting tomorrow, which we cannot grasp, to God. Humility is not passive inaction; it is returning to our rightful place as human beings: I faithfully do what God has entrusted to me today, and let God manage what I cannot manage.
Let people be people, let God be God; let Jesus be King, and the heart finds true rest.

God is not only the Rock himself; verse 7 also says, “You who are upright make the path of the righteous level.” We may not know how the road ahead will go, but we know who is leading us. Faith is not waiting to see the whole road before moving forward, but trusting that God will guide step by step. Take the Bible as our standard, the Holy Spirit as our guide, and fix our eyes on Jesus as we move on; it is not that I must make every road in life level, but that I trust God to lead me on the road he has prepared for me.
a: Fix Your Mind on God
Think less about the problem over and over; think more about God’s faithfulness.
Release What You Can’t Control
Do your part, and entrust the results and tomorrow to God.
Follow God Step by Step
Even when you can’t yet see the road ahead, trust that God will guide.
q: What troubles me most right now? Am I willing to stop trying to control it by myself and truly entrust it to God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, You are my everlasting Rock. Help me keep my focus not on myself, others, or circumstances, but wholly on You. I will lay down my need to control and let Jesus be King in me, and by the Holy Spirit walk the road You lead me on. However circumstances change, let my heart be steadied by trusting You, believing that You will keep me and guide me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will trust steadfastly in Yahweh, and he will keep me in perfect peace!

t: Until He Finds the One
v: He told them this parable.
“Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep, and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?
When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’
I tell you that even so there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.”
b: Jesus uses the parable of the lost sheep to show us the heart of the Heavenly Father. The shepherd has a hundred sheep and loses only one, yet he still goes out to look for it, and he searches “until he finds it.” In human eyes, one may be only one percent; in the shepherd’s heart, that sheep is an irreplaceable life. God does not see people as cold numbers, nor as a measure of who is more useful; every lost person is a life he loves and seeks.
Jesus did not come into the world to wait at a distance for sinners to find their own way home; he came to actively seek the lost.

Even more moving, after the shepherd finds the sheep he does not scold it, “Why did you wander off?” Instead he “carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing.” The lost sheep is exhausted and may not have the strength to walk back, so the shepherd carries it home himself. This is the gospel: not that we return to God by our own strength, but that Jesus finds us and carries us, and brings us home to the Father’s house.

So true shepherding is not merely managing people or making demands on them, but loving, seeking, and walking with people with the life of Jesus the Shepherd. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; don’t easily give up on someone because he is weak or hard to lead.

When one sinner repents, Jesus says, “there will be joy in heaven.” This lets us know that what the Kingdom of God values most is lives being found. The real fruit of the church is not only how many activities are held or how well things are done, but lost people returning to God and lives being changed by Christ. When we lay down our own convenience and gain and loss, and let Jesus be King, the Holy Spirit can place the shepherd’s heart in us, so that we actively go to those in need. Building God’s divine order means cherishing every person with the Father’s heart, and seeking the lost until we find them.
a: Value Every Life
Don’t look down on anyone because of weakness, background, or circumstances.
Actively Seek the Lost
Don’t just wait for people to come back; take the initiative to care, accompany, and restore.
Walk with People with a Shepherd’s Heart
Blame less and support more, bringing people back to Jesus’ side.
q: Is there someone near me whom God is reminding me to actively seek out, care for, and walk with?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for not giving up on me, but through Jesus actively seeking me and bringing me back into Your love. Put the heart of Jesus the Shepherd in me, so that I cherish every life and do not despise or give up on the lost and the weak. Let Jesus be King in me, and by the Holy Spirit help me actively care for, accompany, and seek, so that more people return to Your home, heaven is full of joy, and all glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will go after the lost sheep until I find it, and rejoice over its return!

t: Don’t Forget God in Success
v: You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless Yahweh your God for the good land which he has given you.
“Beware lest you forget Yahweh your God, in not keeping his commandments, and his ordinances, and his statutes, which I command you this day;
lest, when you have eaten and are full, and have built goodly houses, and lived therein;
and when your herds and your flocks multiply, and your silver and your gold is multiplied, and all that you have is multiplied;
then your heart be lifted up, and you forget Yahweh your God, who brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage;
who led you through that great and terrible wilderness, in which were fiery serpents and scorpions, and thirsty ground where was no water; who brought you forth water out of the rock of flint;
who fed you in the wilderness with manna, which your fathers didn’t know; that he might humble you, and that he might prove you, to do you good at your latter end;
and lest you say in your heart, ‘My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth.’
But you shall remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers, as it is this day.”
b: In hardship people easily cry out to God, but in prosperity they easily forget him. Moses warned the Israelites who were about to enter Canaan that the truly dangerous time is not necessarily when they have nothing, but perhaps when they have everything. When houses are better, wealth increases, and life is secure, it is easy to slide from “thanking God” to “I earned this by my own effort.” Scripture points to the root of the problem: “your heart be lifted up, and you forget Yahweh.” Pride is seeing God’s grace as our own merit, and taking the ability God gave us as our own.

So God repeatedly commands, “Remember Yahweh your God.” Remembering is not only recalling the past; it is acknowledging afresh today: all that I have is grace. The Israelites must not forget that God brought them out of Egypt, God provided manna in the wilderness, and God brought water out of the rock. Even verse 18 says, “it is he who gives you power to get wealth.” We can work hard, study, and manage, but even the strength of our bodies, the wisdom of our thoughts, and the opportunities of our work are all given by God. Humility is not denying our effort, but knowing that all our abilities ultimately come from God.

So a person who truly belongs to God is not someone without achievements, but someone who does not let achievements take God’s place; not someone who cannot own things, but someone who does not let “what I own” become the basis for making himself king. God gives me, so I live for God; God lets me gain, so I give the glory to God. When we let go of “my power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth,” we can return to our rightful place as human beings, let God be God, and let Jesus be King. The greatest victory in success is not gaining more, but, having gained everything, still belonging to God in the heart.
a: Be More Thankful When Blessed
Behind every achievement, remember God’s grace.
Stay Humble in Success
Don’t treat the abilities God gave you as your own merit.
Give What You Gain to God’s Use
God gives to you not only for your enjoyment but to accomplish his purposes.
q: Among the achievements, abilities, and resources I now have, is there anything that has begun to make me feel, “I got this by myself”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for leading and providing for me all along the way. Guard my heart, so that I rely on You in lack and all the more do not forget You in abundance. I admit that all my abilities, opportunities, and results are Your grace. Take away my pride, help me lay down self and let Jesus be King; however much You give me and however much I accomplish, let me faithfully use it for You and give all glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will remember Yahweh my God, for it is he who gives me power to get wealth!

t: The Busier You Are, the Closer You Must Draw to God
v: Immediately, when they had come out of the synagogue, they came into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.
Now Simon’s wife’s mother lay sick with a fever, and immediately they told him about her.
He came and took her by the hand, and raised her up. The fever left her, and she served them.
At evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick, and those who were possessed by demons.
All the city was gathered together at the door.
He healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. He didn’t allow the demons to speak, because they knew him.
Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.
Simon and those who were with him followed after him;
and they found him, and told him, “Everyone is looking for you.”
He said to them, “Let’s go elsewhere into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because for this reason I came out.”
He went into their synagogues throughout all Galilee, preaching and casting out demons.
b: Jesus’ day was extremely busy: teaching, healing the sick, casting out demons, and “all the city was gathered together at the door.” Yet the next morning, “while it was still dark,” Jesus left the crowds and went out to a deserted place to pray. He did not let the demands of ministry reduce his fellowship with the Father. This shows us an important order for life: we do not draw near to God after we finish being busy; we draw near to God first, and then we know how we ought to be busy.
The power to serve does not come from busyness; it flows from our relationship with God. Life first, then relationship, then ministry.

When Simon found Jesus he said, “Everyone is looking for you.” Those words stand for enormous need, and also for success and applause. If Jesus had simply followed the needs of the people, he could have stayed where he was and kept on healing. But prayer made the Father’s will clear to him, and so he answered, “Let’s go elsewhere… because for this reason I came out.” Not every need is a call from God, and not every opportunity is something God wants us to do.
The voices of people say, “Everyone needs you,” but prayer lets us hear “what God truly wants you to do.” The focus is not on people or on tasks, but on the will of God.

Jesus himself set the example for us: first connect with the Father, then enter into service. True ministry that belongs to God is not carried on by brains, ability, and zeal alone, but by seeking the guidance of the Holy Spirit, understanding God’s heart, and then going forward in reliance on the Lord. When we lay down the self-centered life of “everything depends on me” and let Jesus be King, we are no longer pulled around by busyness, social pressure, and expectations. Prayer brings us back from the needs of people to the will of God, and from our own strength to God’s strength. It is not that I am busy for God, but that God accomplishes through me what he wants to do.
a: The Busier, the More You Pray
Don’t wait until the work is done to draw near to God; draw near to him first, and then go to work.
Tell a Need from a Calling
Don’t be pulled around by everyone’s expectations; first seek God’s true heart.
Let Service Flow from Life
Don’t grit your teeth and push on in your own strength; let Jesus be King and rely on the Holy Spirit to carry out each day’s assignment.
q: Is my present busyness what God truly wants me to do, or am I being pushed along by people’s expectations and my own sense of duty?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, help me to follow Jesus’ example and keep drawing near to You first, even in the midst of busyness. Keep me from being pulled around by people’s needs, expectations, and circumstances. Instead, let me seek Your will in prayer and be sensitive to the guidance of the Holy Spirit. I want to lay down the life that relies on myself and let Jesus be King in me, so that my service flows from my relationship with You, and I complete the work You truly entrusted to me, giving all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will follow Jesus, go to a quiet place to pray, understand God’s will, and complete what he has entrusted to me!

t: Place Yourself in God’s Hands
v: The word which came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying,
“Arise, and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will cause you to hear my words.”
Then I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was doing his work on the wheels.
When the vessel that he made of the clay was marred in the hand of the potter, he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.
Then the word of Yahweh came to me, saying,
“House of Israel, can’t I do with you as this potter? says Yahweh. Behold, as the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel.
At what instant I speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy it;
if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to them.
At what instant I speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it;
if they do that which is evil in my sight, that they not obey my voice, then I will repent of the good, with which I said I would benefit them.”
b: God brought Jeremiah to the potter’s house to show him a living picture: the clay was in the potter’s hand, and the potter made it “as seemed good to the potter.” This passage is first of all what God said to the nation of Israel, declaring his sovereignty over nations; but it also shows us an important principle: God is the potter and we are the clay. He has sovereignty, and we should submit to him.

The greatest problem people have is often wanting to climb from the clay’s place into the potter’s seat, demanding that God shape their lives according to their own wishes. Humility is returning to our rightful place: letting people be people, letting God be God, and letting Jesus be King.

What is even more precious is that when the vessel was “marred,” the potter did not immediately throw the clay away, but “made it again another vessel.” This does not mean that sin and rebellion have no consequences; it shows us that as long as we remain in the potter’s hand, there is still the possibility of being formed anew. Verse 8 points out in particular that if people “turn from their evil,” God will not bring the disaster he had announced. Failure need not be the final verdict on a life; repentance can become the starting point of being reshaped.
God does not want merely to patch up our outward behavior; he wants to reshape our lives from within, so that we become more and more like Christ.

What makes clay into a useful vessel is not that the clay decides its own shape, but that it stays soft and stays in the potter’s hands. When we insist on “how I want it,” our lives easily become hard; when we lay ourselves down and say, “Lord, shape me as you please,” the Holy Spirit can work within us. God sometimes builds and sometimes tears down, sometimes plants and sometimes plucks up, but what he wants is not to fulfill our own blueprint, but to accomplish his will. Selflessness is not losing ourselves; it is giving ourselves wholly to God, so that we become useful vessels in his hands.
a: Return to Your Rightful Place
Don’t demand that God do things your way; learn to submit to his sovereignty.
Return to God’s Hands After Failure
Don’t stay under condemnation; repent sincerely and let God reshape your life.
Keep a Soft, Teachable Heart
Accept God’s correction and adjustment, and let the Holy Spirit shape you into a vessel that fits God’s heart.
q: In my life, where am I still insisting on “it must be done my way,” unwilling to place myself fully in God’s hands?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, You are the potter and I am the clay in Your hands. Please remove my pride, my hardness, and my self-centeredness, and bring me back to my rightful place as a human being, so that You are God and Jesus is King. Even though my life has known failure, please give me true repentance and bring me back into Your hands. May the Holy Spirit keep shaping me, making me more and more like Jesus, a useful vessel in Your hands, carrying out Your will, so that all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am clay in God’s hands, and I will let him shape me as seems good to him!

t: Accept One Another and Glorify God in Unity
v: Now the God of patience and of encouragement grant you to be of the same mind one with another according to Christ Jesus;
that with one accord you may with one mouth glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.
For I say that Christ has been made a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, that he might confirm the promises given to the fathers,
and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, “Therefore I will give praise to you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.”
Again he says, “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.”
Again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles! Let all the peoples praise him.”
Again, Isaiah says, “There will be the root of Jesse, he who arises to rule over the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.”
Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope, in the power of the Holy Spirit.
b: Paul says, “Be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus.” Being of the same mind does not mean that everyone has exactly the same personality, opinions, and ways of doing things; it means that in our differences we share Christ as our common center. When everyone insists on “doing it my way,” differences easily become conflicts; but when everyone turns their focus to Jesus and sets aside the self on the throne, we can build one another up in Christ. True unity is not everyone becoming like me, but everyone becoming more and more like Jesus.
Selflessness makes unity possible, because when “I” am no longer the center, Christ can become our common center.

So Paul goes on: “Accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you.” The basis on which we accept others is not that they fully match our expectations, but that Christ has already accepted us. Acceptance does not mean agreeing with every error; it means continuing, within the truth, to love people, respect them, and walk with them. When we remember how the Lord has been patient with us, forgiven us, and accepted us, we can treat others with the same grace. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; don’t hurt someone Christ loves just to prove that you are right.

The final purpose of unity is not to build a group that feels good together, but that “with one accord you may with one mouth glorify God.” From Jew to Gentile, God’s salvation makes people of different backgrounds one new community in Christ, praising God together. This cannot be done by human tolerance techniques alone, but “in the power of the Holy Spirit.” When we follow Jesus’ example, take the Bible as our standard, and let the Holy Spirit guide us, Jesus is King among us. Moving from accepting one another to being of one mind, and from being of one mind to glorifying God with one mouth, is the beautiful testimony of God’s people.
a: Make Christ Our Common Center
Don’t demand that everyone do things my way; seek the Lord’s heart together.
Accept People as Christ Does
Love, bear with, and build up others within the truth.
Live Out Unity by the Holy Spirit
Set yourself aside and let Jesus be King, so that we glorify God with one accord and one mouth.
q: In my relationships, is there someone I find very hard to accept? Am I willing to think about how Christ accepted me, and to accept that person with his grace?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for accepting me in Christ. Help me follow Jesus, lay down my stubbornness and pride, and stop demanding that others do things my way. Fill me with the Holy Spirit, so that I may accept and build up others with Christ’s love and remain of one mind in spite of our differences. May Jesus be King among us, so that with one accord and one mouth we glorify You, and abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: By the power of the Holy Spirit I will abound in hope, and glorify God with one accord and one mouth together with my brothers and sisters!

t: Honor Christ as Lord in Your Heart
v: Now who is he who will harm you, if you become imitators of that which is good?
But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. “Don’t be afraid of their threats, neither be troubled.”
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts; and always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear:
having a good conscience; that, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be put to shame who curse your good way of life in Christ.
For it is better, if it is God’s will, that you suffer for doing well than for doing evil.
b: Peter wrote to believers who were under pressure and hostility. He did not promise that following Jesus means we will never suffer; instead he said, “Even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed.” The greater the pressure, the more clearly it shows who is truly king of our lives. When people are king, we easily fear their opinions, threats, and criticism; when Christ is King, we can still choose the right path under pressure. True victory is not having no one oppose me, but still faithfully following Jesus even when people do.

Peter gives the most important answer to fear: “Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts.” This does not only mean confessing Jesus with the mouth, but acknowledging him as Lord in the deepest part of our lives. Why are people afraid? Often because other people’s opinions, our own gains and losses, or our circumstances have taken the throne in our hearts. When the focus returns to Jesus and we let him be King, we no longer need to argue, prove ourselves, or protect ourselves. It is not that circumstances change first and then the heart has peace; it is that Christ is King in the heart first, and then we can stand firm in the midst of circumstances.

When others ask us for “a reason concerning the hope that is in you,” Peter does not tell us to win the argument with a hard attitude, but to answer everyone “with humility and fear,” and to bear witness to the gospel by our “good way of life in Christ.” A truly powerful witness is not only what we say, but what others see in us. When we let Jesus be King, gentleness can overcome confrontation, a good life can overcome slander, and our lives can prove the gospel.
When people see Christ in us, all the glory naturally goes to God.
a: Don’t Fear What People Think
Even when opposed, keep choosing to do what pleases God.
Let Christ Be King in Your Heart
Don’t let people’s opinions and circumstances control your heart.
Witness to the Gospel with Your Life
Answer people with gentleness and live out Christ through a good life.
q: Whose opinion, judgment, or pressure do I fear right now, so that I have not fully let Christ be King in my heart?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, whatever circumstances I face, help me honor Christ as Lord in my heart. Help me not to fear what people think or their threats, and not to rely on arguing and proving myself, but to let Jesus be King in me. Holy Spirit, enable me to witness to the gospel with gentleness, reverence, and a beautiful life, and even if I suffer for doing right, to keep faithfully doing good, so that people see Christ in my life and all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will honor Christ the Lord as holy in my heart, not fearing threats and not being troubled!

t: Don’t Just Love the Plant; Love the People God Loves
v: God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil which he said he would do to them, and he didn’t do it.

He prayed to Yahweh, and said, “Please, Yahweh, wasn’t this what I said when I was still in my country? Therefore I hurried to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and one who relents from sending calamity.
Yahweh said, “Is it right for you to be angry?”
Yahweh God prepared a vine, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to deliver him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the vine.
But God prepared a worm when the next day dawned, and it attacked the vine, so that it withered.

When the sun arose, God prepared a sultry east wind; and the sun beat on Jonah’s head, so that he fainted, and requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”
God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the vine?” He said, “It is right for me to be angry, even to death.”
Yahweh said, “You have had pity on the vine, for which you have not labored, neither made it grow, which came up in a night, and perished in a night.
Shouldn’t I have pity on Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also many animals?”
b: Jonah’s biggest problem was not that he did not know God, but that his heart was not yet in line with God’s heart. He knew perfectly well that God is “gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness,” yet he became angry because God forgave the people of Nineveh. Jonah wanted God to deal with Nineveh the way he thought best, but God wanted Jonah to learn to see Nineveh through his heart. This reminds us: knowing God’s truth is not the same as having God’s heart.
Truth must not only enter our minds but our lives; only when our viewpoint changes can our mindset change, from “how do I see this person?” to “how does God see this person?”

God provided a vine to shade Jonah, and Jonah was exceedingly glad; when the vine withered, he was so angry he asked to die. Through that vine God exposed what Jonah really valued: he cared for a plant that made him comfortable, but not for the lives of more than one hundred twenty thousand people in a city. The self-centered life easily worries about “what is in it for me,” while God’s heart cares about “can this person be saved?”

We too may care deeply about our own convenience, rights, feelings, and gains and losses, while overlooking the people around us who truly need the gospel, care, and rescue. People matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things, and a life matters far more than a “vine.”

In the end the book of Jonah does not tell us how Jonah answered; it stops on one question from God: “Shouldn’t I have pity?” That question is also addressed to us. What God wants to change is not only the wickedness of the Ninevites, but also Jonah’s narrow heart. True service is not reluctantly doing things for God, but letting Jesus be King so that we begin to love the people God loves. Selflessness means no longer asking only “do I like it?” but asking, “Lord, whom do you love? Whom do you want me to love?”
When we have the Father’s heart, we will not see only our own vine, but will also see the Nineveh waiting for the gospel.
a: See People with God’s Eyes
Don’t judge people by your likes and dislikes, but see that every life is loved by God.
Examine Your Own “Vine”
Don’t let your convenience, interests, and feelings matter more than people’s lives.
Love the People God Loves
Set yourself aside and take the initiative to care for, walk with, and bring the gospel to those in need.
q: Is there any “vine” in my life that I care about so much that it matters more to me than the people God loves?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, please give me Your heart, so that I not only know Your truth but also love the people You love. Shine Your light on me, that I may see the places where I think only of my own convenience, interests, and feelings. I want to set myself aside and let Jesus be King. Holy Spirit, enlarge my heart so that I see the lost, care for the hurting, and bring the gospel to those in need. May my heart beat with Your heart, so that all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will have compassion on the people God loves and see every precious life with God’s heart!

t: Drop the Nets and Follow Jesus
v: Walking by the sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and Andrew, his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
He said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.”
They immediately left their nets, and followed him.
Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them.
They immediately left the boat and their father, and followed him.
b: When Jesus called Peter and Andrew, his first words were not “Go and do something for me,” but “Follow me.” This reveals the most important order in a disciple’s life: first follow Jesus, then do things for Jesus; first life, then relationship, then ministry.

The most important calling of a Christian is not how much work we complete, but to follow Jesus and become like Jesus every day, letting him change us. When our lives truly keep pace with the Lord, service will naturally flow out of our lives.

Peter and Andrew “immediately left their nets,” and James and John also “immediately left the boat,” and followed Jesus. The “nets” and the “boat” were not sinful in themselves; they were what the men depended on for their living and with which they held their lives in their own hands. The key to following Jesus is who holds the highest authority over our lives. Today our “nets” may be money, achievement, status, habits, our own plans, or even “it must be done my way.” Denying ourselves does not mean having nothing; it means no longer letting anything take the place of Jesus. Set the self down from the throne, and let Jesus be King.

Jesus did not only say “follow me”; he also promised, “I will make you fishers of men.” Notice: it is not that the disciples turn themselves into fishers of men by their own effort, but that Jesus says, “I will make you.” Our responsibility is to follow him; the one who changes, equips, and uses our lives is the Lord. When we take Jesus as our example, the Bible as our standard, and the Holy Spirit as our guide, we can move from a life lived only for ourselves into a life lived for God and for others. A true disciple is not someone who merely walks behind Jesus, but someone who is changed by Jesus and in the end brings others along to follow him as well.
a: Follow Jesus Every Day
First ask, “Lord, how do you want me to follow you?” then ask, “What shall I do today?”
Drop Your Own “Nets”
Identify what is hardest to let go of in your life and don’t let it replace Jesus as King.
From Following to Leading Others
Let your life be changed by Jesus, and walk with others to become the Lord’s disciples too.
q: What “net” am I still gripping tightly today that keeps me from fully following Jesus?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for calling me through Jesus to follow him. Help me not only to do things for You, but to draw near to Jesus and become like Jesus every day. Holy Spirit, shine Your light on me so that I am willing to let go of the “nets” I cling to, no longer crowning myself, but letting Jesus be King in me. Lord, shape my life so that I not only follow You myself, but also walk with many others to know You and follow You, so that all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will drop my nets at once and follow Jesus, and let him make me a disciple who fishes for people!

t: Don’t Make Someone Else’s Failure Your Opportunity
v: It happened in the eleventh year, in the first day of the month, that the word of Yahweh came to me, saying,
“Son of man, because Tyre has said against Jerusalem, ‘Aha! She is broken who was the gateway of the peoples; she is turned to me; I will be replenished, now that she is laid waste;’
therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I am against you, Tyre, and will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea causes its waves to come up.
They will destroy the walls of Tyre, and break down her towers. I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her a bare rock.
She will be a place for the spreading of nets in the middle of the sea; for I have spoken it, says the Lord Yahweh. She will become a plunder to the nations.
Her daughters who are in the field will be slain by the sword. Then they will know that I am Yahweh.”

They will take up a lamentation over you, and tell you, ‘How you are destroyed, who were inhabited by seafaring men, the renowned city, who was strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, who caused their terror to be on all who lived there!
Now the islands will tremble in the day of your fall. Yes, the islands that are in the sea will be dismayed at your departure.’”
b: Tyre was an important maritime trading city of that time. When Jerusalem was destroyed, Tyre did not grieve for her, but said instead, “She is laid waste; I will be replenished.” Someone else’s disaster became, in Tyre’s eyes, her own business opportunity. This exposes a self-centered life: it asks only, “What is in this for me?” and never asks, “What pain is someone else bearing?”

The self-centered life easily sees others as competitors, and when others fail it may even secretly rejoice. But the life that pleases God does not climb up by stepping on others’ failure; it has the compassionate heart of Christ and weeps with those who weep.

Tyre’s greatest mistake was not only commercial competition, but proudly building her own prosperity on the ruin of others. She was once a “renowned city,” strong and prosperous on the sea, and it seemed that no one could shake her; yet God declared, “I am against you.” This is a very sober reminder: the greatest danger to people is not losing success, but leaving our rightful place in the midst of success and thinking we can control everything.
Pride lifts a person up; humility returns a person to their place, letting people be people and God be God. True security is not in wealth, status, or power, but in fearing God and relying on God.

In the end, that city that amazed everyone became a thing everyone lamented. Earthly success, wealth, and power can all change; only God and his Kingdom last forever. So let us not build “my own system,” but let Jesus be King and build God’s divine order. Success that truly pleases God is not that I prosper more than others, but that God gives me the ability to build others up; it is not taking advantage of other people’s breaches, but helping others repair them.
When we turn from “I want to get” to “I want to give,” and from competing to building others up, we live out more and more of the life of Christ.
a: Don’t Gloat
When you see others fail, don’t compare or judge; show compassion and lend a hand.
Stay Humble in Success
Don’t boast of wealth, ability, or achievement; see everything as God’s grace.
From Competing to Building Up
Don’t climb by stepping on others; use the resources God gave you to help others stand up.
q: When another person’s failure might benefit me, is my first thought of my own opportunity, or of that person’s real need?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, remove from me the pride, selfishness, and gloating in my heart, so that I do not treat other people’s failure as my opportunity. Give me Jesus’ compassion, so that I do not compete with people but build them up. I want to set myself aside and let Jesus be King; the ability, resources, and achievements You have given me, I want to use to bless others and build up lives, so that all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will humbly rely on Yahweh, not rejoice in the failure of others, but use everything God has given me to build others up!

t: Meet Jesus, and Your Life Turns Around
v: But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest,
and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
As he traveled, it happened that he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him.
He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”
He said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But rise up, and enter into the city, and it will be told you what you must do.”

Ananias departed, and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the way which you came, has sent me, that you may receive your sight, and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.
He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.
Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God.
b: Saul was firmly convinced that he was on the right road, and even carried the high priest’s authorization to Damascus to arrest Christians. Yet right on that road he met the risen Jesus, and suddenly discovered that the direction he was most sure of was entirely wrong.

The greatest problem a person has is sometimes not a lack of zeal but a zeal centered on self; not a lack of direction, but deciding the direction oneself. Saul set out to seize people, but Jesus seized him first. Real change in life begins with meeting Jesus; when the focus turns from “what I think” to “what the Lord says,” the direction of life begins to change.

After falling to the ground, Saul asked, “Who are you, Lord?” Then Jesus told him, “Rise up, and enter into the city, and it will be told you what you must do.” In the past Saul decided for himself “what I will do”; now he began to learn, “Lord, what do you want me to do?” This is the transfer of lordship over a life. Repentance is not only stopping doing wrong; it is turning from crowning oneself to letting Jesus be King.
Pride is leaving our rightful place and deciding good and evil and direction for ourselves; humility is returning to our place, acknowledging that Jesus is Lord, and letting him decide my path.

Later Ananias laid his hands on Saul, and his eyes received sight and he was filled with the Holy Spirit. The one who once persecuted Jesus soon began to proclaim “the Christ, that he is the Son of God.” This is the power of the gospel to change lives: Jesus not only forgives our past but can turn our future around; he not only rescues us from our mistakes but makes us vessels in his hands.
When we let Jesus be King and are filled with the Holy Spirit, a person who lived for himself can be transformed into a person who lives for Jesus, so that all the glory goes to him.
a: Meet Jesus Anew Every Day
Don’t rely only on your own experience and judgment; return to the Lord often and seek him.
Hand Over Lordship of Your Life
Ask less “What shall I do?” and more “Lord, what do you want me to do?”
Let Your Past Become a Testimony
Don’t be limited by past failures; believe that Jesus can renew, change, and use us.
q: Is there an area of my life that is still “my own decision,” where I have not truly asked Jesus, “Lord, what do you want me to do?”
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for seeking and saving me through Jesus, and for being ready to change my life. Help me no longer insist on my own way, but humbly return to Your presence. I want to lay down my own authority and let Jesus be King in me. Fill and guide me, Holy Spirit, so that I see what You see and walk the road You want me to walk, completing the mission You have entrusted to me, so that my whole life bears witness to Jesus and all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will let Jesus be my Lord, be filled with the Holy Spirit, and proclaim all my life that Jesus is the Son of God!

t: Lose Everything, Yet Still Worship God
v: It fell on a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother’s house,
that there came a messenger to Job, and said, “The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys feeding beside them,
and the Sabeans attacked, and took them away. Yes, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you.”

While he was still speaking, there also came another, and said, “The fire of God has fallen from the sky, and has burned up the sheep and the servants, and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you.”

While he was still speaking, there came also another, and said, “The Chaldeans made three bands, and swept down on the camels, and have taken them away, yes, and killed the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you.”
While he was still speaking, there came also another, and said, “Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother’s house,
and behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on the young men, and they are dead. I alone have escaped to tell you.”
Then Job arose, and tore his robe, and shaved his head, and fell down on the ground, and worshiped.
He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be the name of Yahweh.”
In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God with wrongdoing.
b: Disaster after disaster fell on Job; before one messenger had finished speaking, the next arrived. In a very short time he lost his livestock, his property, his servants, and finally even all his children. Job did not pretend that he was not in pain; he “tore his robe and shaved his head,” which were ways of expressing the deepest grief in that time. Biblical faith does not deny pain, nor does it require us to pretend to be strong in sorrow. True faith can weep and still not leave God; it can fail to understand and still choose to trust God.

The most astonishing thing is that in the extremity of his pain Job “fell down on the ground and worshiped.” He had no answers yet, and did not know what was happening in heaven, but he still acknowledged, “Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away.” This does not mean that every disaster can be simply understood as directly caused by God; it means that within his limited understanding, Job still acknowledged that all of life is ultimately under God’s sovereignty. The highest level of faith is not worshiping God only because he has blessed me, but still honoring him as God even when I cannot understand what is happening.
Let people be people and God be God; I can be without answers and still let God be King.

Job finally said, “Blessed be the name of Yahweh.” Circumstances had changed completely, but God’s place in his life had not changed. This shows the core of true worship: we worship God not only because of what he has given us, but because he is God. When we lay down the self-centered life of “God must bless me the way I want,” we can move from grasping God’s gifts to grasping God himself. True victory is not never losing; it is, even in losing, not losing God. It is not praising only when I have everything, but knowing that with the Lord I still have hope.
a: You Can Weep in Pain
You need not pretend to be strong; bring your real hurt before God.
Trust Even When You Don’t Understand
Don’t rush to explain everything for God; admit your limits and believe God is still in control.
From the Gift to the Giver
Love God not only for the blessings he gives, but worship him because he himself is your treasure.
q: If God does not accomplish things the way I expect, will I still trust him, love him, and let him be King in my life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, when I meet things I cannot understand, please keep my heart fixed on You. I admit my limits and bring my pain, questions, and tears to You. Whatever the circumstances, I am willing to let You be God and let Jesus be King. Holy Spirit, hold me up, so that I give thanks in good times, trust in hard times, and worship You in every situation. You Yourself are my greatest blessing; may my life bring glory to Your name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Whether I gain or lose, I will bless the name of Yahweh!

t: Walk by the Spirit and Live Out Christ
v: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the lust of the flesh.
For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.
But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
Now the works of the flesh are obvious, which are: adultery, sexual immorality, uncleanness, lustfulness,
idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions, heresies,
envyings, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these; of which I forewarn you, even as I also forewarned you, that those who practice such things will not inherit the Kingdom of God.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
b: Paul points out that there is a real battle in the Christian life: “The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.” Here “the flesh” does not mean only the body, but the tendency of fallen human nature to live apart from God, centered on self. It shows itself in hatred, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, rivalries, and divisions. The root of the problem is often not the outward conflict but what is inside: whether “self is king” or “God is king.” The real spiritual battle takes place first within us; victory is not changing others first, but letting the Holy Spirit change me first.

Paul does not tell us to suppress the flesh by willpower alone, but says, “Walk by the Spirit,” and, “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” A branch does not strive to produce fruit; it is connected to the source of life and bears fruit naturally. In the same way, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control are not nine character goals to be achieved by effort, but the fruit borne when the Holy Spirit reigns in a person’s life.
The Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide, and Jesus is my example; it is not that I strive to act like Christ by my own effort, but that the Holy Spirit lives out Christ within me.

So verse 24 brings us back to the cross: “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.” The gospel is not about improving the old self; it is about new life in Christ. Each day, facing emotions, conflict, temptation, and choices, we can set down “I want it my way” and choose to let Jesus be King and submit to the Spirit. Selflessness does not mean having no self; it means no longer letting self be king. It is not that I live out nine kinds of fruit by my own effort, but that Christ lives in me and the Spirit naturally bears the fruit of Christ’s life.
a: Deal with Yourself First, Then the Situation
When angry, jealous, or in conflict, first ask yourself: is the flesh reacting now, or is the Spirit leading?
Walk by the Spirit Every Day
In each choice, pause and ask, “Holy Spirit, how do you want me to respond?”
Let Your Life Bear Fruit
Don’t only pursue doing more; value becoming more and more full of the life of Jesus.
q: Which kind of fleshly reaction appears most easily in my life lately? How can I set myself aside in this matter and submit to the Holy Spirit’s guidance?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for giving me new life through the cross of Jesus. Shine Your light on me so that I see the self-centeredness, jealousy, anger, rivalry, and every fleshly reaction within me. I give myself to You again and let Jesus be King in me. Fill and guide me, Holy Spirit, that I may act not on my own but by the Spirit, bearing the fruit of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control, living out Christ, so that all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will live by the Spirit, walk by the Spirit, and bear the fruit of the Spirit!

t: Rooted for a Lifetime, Fruitful for a Lifetime
v: (A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath day.) It is a good thing to give thanks to Yahweh, to sing praises to your name, Most High;
to proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night,
[Combined with the previous verse]
For you, Yahweh, have made me glad through your work. I will triumph in the works of your hands.
How great are your works, Yahweh! Your thoughts are very deep.
The righteous will flourish like the palm tree. He will grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
They are planted in Yahweh’s house. They will flourish in our God’s courts.
They will still produce fruit in old age. They will be full of sap and green,
to show that Yahweh is upright. He is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.
b: The psalmist says, “Proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night.” A day begins with God’s loving kindness and ends in his faithfulness. The true joy of spiritual life is not only that things develop the way we expect, but that we increasingly see “the works of Yahweh.” When our focus stays on ourselves, we easily count our gains and losses; when our focus turns to God, we find there is grace to be thankful for every day. Looking to his loving kindness in the morning and counting his faithfulness at night, over time thankfulness becomes a habit of life.

The psalmist describes the righteous as those who “flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon,” and the key is in the next verse: “They are planted in Yahweh’s house.” Whether a tree flourishes for a long time depends not only on how tall it looks on the outside, but on where its roots are. People’s achievements, abilities, and positions all change; only God is the eternal rock. Life must first be rooted before it can grow; life must first be connected to God before it can bear true fruit.
So: life first, then relationship, then ministry. Don’t first pursue how much you can do for God, but first let your life be deeply rooted in God.

What is more precious: “They will still produce fruit in old age; they will be full of sap and green.” In God’s Kingdom, old age is not the end of a life’s worth, but can be a season of greater maturity and abundance. What God wants is not a brief brilliance but lifelong faithfulness; not serving only while we are young and strong, but living out Christ and blessing others even into old age. When we let Jesus be King and let the Holy Spirit keep renewing our lives, we can bear fruit all our lives. The real success of life is not only living long, but still bearing the fruit of Christ’s life to the very end, so that people see in us: “Yahweh is upright; he is my rock.”
a: Count God’s Grace Morning and Night
In the morning think of God’s loving kindness; in the evening recall his faithfulness through the day.
Let Your Life Be Deeply Rooted in God
Don’t pursue only ministry results; value your real relationship with God every day.
Bear Fruit All Your Life
At whatever stage of life, let the Holy Spirit live out Christ through you and bless others.
q: If my life is a tree, where am I really rooted now? As the years go by, am I bearing more and more of the fruit of Christ’s life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You that Your loving kindness is new every day and Your faithfulness lasts forever. Root my life deeply in You, so that I rely not on myself, my achievements, or my circumstances, but on You as my eternal rock. I want to let Jesus be King; Holy Spirit, renew me every day, so that I flourish all my life and still bear fruit even in old age, witnessing to Your faithfulness with my life, so that all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am planted in Yahweh’s house; I will still bear fruit in old age, full of sap and green!
